groups.title: Slider
groups.lede: Base slider grips. Neutral shapes where the release, not the grip, decides gyro vs. sweep vs. slutter.

items.name: SL1 — Standard Offset
items.grip: Set it like a tight four-seam, then slide both fingers to one side of the ball so the pads sit on the seam. Thumb underneath. The hand stays close to a fastball's, which is the whole idea.
items.movement: Sits 4-7 off the fastball in the slutter/gyro window. Low HB, mostly bullet spin — the release, not the grip, decides how much cut shows up.
items.when: Reach for it when a pitcher wants to hold fastball velo and intent and let his natural finish carve the cut. The easiest breaking ball to fold into a heater delivery.
items.watch: Almost no seam leverage for sweep — if you want real HB, move to a two-seam orientation like SL3 or SL6.

items.name: SL2 — Standard
items.grip: Fingers just off-center between the inner seams: middle finger flat on a seam, index resting on the leather. Thumb rides the opposite side, off-center. The ring-finger knuckle braces the side for control and the pinky comes off.
items.movement: 6-10 off the fastball. Neutral axis out of the hand — the finish determines whether it plays gyro or sweep. Middle finger drives the spin.
items.when: The default slider to build off of. Good when you don't yet know a pitcher's release bias and want a blank shape to shape.
items.watch: Neutral by design, so it gives back exactly what the release supplies and nothing more.

items.name: SL3 — Standard Around
items.grip: Same inner-seam placement as SL2 but slid up toward the horseshoe, so there's more seam under the fingers to pull around. Middle-finger pressure does the pulling; thumb underneath.
items.movement: 7-11 off the fastball with more HB than SL2. Leans sweeper for pitchers who naturally get to the outside of the ball.
items.when: For a supinator who wants to add sweep to a baseline slider without changing slot.
items.watch: Lean too hard on the index and the axis tips up into slurve territory instead of staying a sweeper.

items.name: Jacob Misiorowski — low across the seams at the horseshoe
items.grip: Index and middle set low and across the seams near the horseshoe, thumb underneath. A hard-slider hold built for velo over shape.
items.movement: A cutter-hard shape that averages mid-90s and tops near 97 — only a few ticks under his fastball. Movement is modest for the velo.
items.when: For a power arm who wants a strike-first breaking ball he can pour in the zone like a cutter.
items.watch: The velo comes at the cost of whiff — a hard, tight shape gets a lot of it in the zone but doesn't miss many barrels.

items.name: Randy Rodríguez — sweeping slider, semi-tucked thumb
items.grip: Fingers on the horseshoe with the thumb only half tucked underneath rather than flat. The half-tuck is the adjustment that changes the shape.
items.movement: Semi-tucking the thumb adds ride year over year — a few inches of IVB — while holding a high whiff rate. Trades some depth for that ride and velo.
items.when: For a two-pitch reliever who has to land the breaking ball for strikes and wants a firmer, higher-riding sweep.
items.watch: The thumb tuck buys ride by giving up depth — fine here because the pitch lives on landing in the zone, not on drop.

items.name: Tyler Rogers — submarine riser slider
items.grip: Not really a slider hold — take a conventional overhand curveball grip, curl it the way you would for an over-the-top curve, and throw it from a submarine slot. The grip is ordinary; the slot is the whole pitch.
items.movement: Released barely a foot off the ground, the inverted arm turns curveball topspin into backspin plus sweep, so the ball climbs all the way and can finish several inches above the plate.
items.when: For a true submariner whose whole arsenal is inverted — sliders up, fastball down — leaving hitters no reference to time.
items.watch: It's a delivery, not a grip: you can't bolt it onto a normal slot. Submarine slots carry heavy platoon splits and a low velo ceiling, and the effect fades with repeat looks.

items.name: Carlos Rodón — cross-horseshoe slider (LHP)
items.grip: Fingers ride the smooth leather above both horseshoes like a two-seamer rather than hooking a single seam, and the spin cuts straight across the seams. The middle finger on the far horseshoe supplies the late leverage.
items.movement: Baseline around 8 inches of HB with vertical break near or just under zero; he can crank it out to 12-13 inches of sweep or trade some in for drop.
items.when: For a supinator who wants a slider that holds near-fastball spin orientation out of the hand and tunnels tight off the four-seam before the late break.
items.watch: With no seam to hook it's very feel-dependent — small hand-position changes swing the shape across a 5-inch range. Rough for a pitcher who needs seam feedback to repeat.

items.name: Garrett Richards — kickstand-index slider
items.grip: Standard slider seam placement, but the index finger comes off as a force contributor — thumb and middle finger are the only pressure points, and the index just leans on the side of the middle finger as a brace. Held firm but not choked, working out over the front and ripping down off the top horseshoe seam.
items.movement: Tilted rather than lateral — not a 12-6, but more downward tilt than a side-to-side slider.
items.when: A middle ground for a pitcher who wants spike-like middle-finger dominance but loses feel when the index leaves the ball entirely.
items.watch: This is a tilted, depth-biased slider, not a sweeper — don't expect glove-side HB out of it.

items.name: Yu Darvish — spiked slider
items.grip: A slider orientation thrown with the index finger spiked into the ball. It came out of a failed knuckle-curve copy — the spike stayed, the slider seam stayed, and it became a second, distinct slider in the same arsenal.
items.movement: Lives in his slider family as a harder-biting shape; the related spiked look tilts roughly 45 degrees down.
items.when: For a deep arsenal that already has a conventional slider and wants a second one with more bite off the same slot and arm action. Spiking is the pronator's route to slider depth.
items.watch: Only worth carrying if you have a standard slider to differentiate it from, and it demands real spike comfort.

groups.title: Slurve
groups.lede: Slider/curve hybrids — sweep with added depth. Built off breaking-ball orientations with index pressure.

items.name: Slurve via index pressure (SL3 base)
items.grip: The SL3 Standard Around placement — fingers up toward the horseshoe between the inner seams — but with deliberate index-finger pressure added at release.
items.movement: 8-12 off the fastball, sitting between the slider and curve clusters. The index pressure tips the spin direction up, giving two-plane break with more velo than a true curve.
items.when: For a supinator who wants a curve's depth without dropping all the way to curve velo.
items.watch: It gives up the sharpness of a true sweeper and tends to land in the softer part of the results plot — a compromise shape, not a plus one.

items.name: Zack Wheeler — slurve (curveball side)
items.grip: Closer to a curveball than a slider: a standard curve hold with the middle finger riding the long seam, index tucked alongside, thumb underneath on the back seam. Nothing spiked.
items.movement: Around 80 with roughly a foot of drop and a foot of sweep, high whiff. From a low slot most breaking balls flatten into sweepers, so the notable part is that he still pulls real depth out of curveball intent.
items.when: For a low-slot arm who wants two-plane shape and is willing to throw a genuine curve to earn the drop.
items.watch: From this low a slot the sweep comes free and the depth has to be earned — back off the curveball intent and it flattens into a sweeper.

items.name: José Soriano — slurve (knuckle-curve grip)
items.grip: A traditional knuckle-curve hold: index finger spiked with the nail dug into the leather, middle finger along the seam, thumb underneath.
items.movement: Around 85 with about a foot of sweep and a few inches of drop — one of the hardest true slurve shapes going. The same grip is a 12-6 for other arms; a low arm angle tilts it toward sweep without changing the hand.
items.when: For a lower-slot pitcher who wants to spike a knuckle-curve grip and let the slot turn it horizontal rather than manufacturing the sweep.
items.watch: It's already flatter than a classic knuckle curve, and the depth keeps shrinking as the velo climbs.

groups.title: Sweeper
groups.lede: Seam-leveraged breaking balls built for horizontal. Grip and seam contact supply the sweep so the arm does not have to.

items.name: Sweeper 1 — Inside Horseshoe
items.grip: Two-seam orientation with the fingers set on the inside of the horseshoe, positioning the seams to drive seam-shifted wake. Thumb underneath.
items.movement: 8-12 off the fastball. The HB arrives late off SSW rather than early Magnus, with little depth.
items.when: For a supinator who can get down and through the bottom outside corner of the ball and wants big glove-side break from a normal slot.
items.watch: Sweepers aren't for every arm — forcing the finish can drive compensations and PCU load, so don't chase it if the release fights it.

items.name: Sweeper 2 — Outside Horseshoe
items.grip: Same two-seam sweeper idea, but the fingers sit on the outside of the horseshoe instead of the inside. Alternate seam contact for the same effect.
items.movement: 8-12 off the fastball in the same window as the inside-horseshoe version — the SSW-driven sweep is identical.
items.when: Try it when the inside-horseshoe hold doesn't feel natural; the movement target is the same, so let comfort pick.
items.watch: Nothing new to trade off here — the two grips are interchangeable and the choice is purely feel.

items.name: Sweeper 3 — Split Two-Seam (“Whirlybird”)
items.grip: Two-seam orientation with the index and middle split apart, and the outer edges of both fingers pressing against the seams instead of sitting on top of them. The seam contact, not the release, does the work.
items.movement: 8-11 off the fastball and holds velo best of the three — the split-seam contact generates the sweep so you don't have to manipulate the finish. The Skenes version sits around 6 inches of IVB with a solid whiff rate.
items.when: For a hard thrower who wants to keep fastball intent and let the grip supply the shape rather than getting around the ball.
items.watch: A wide split can cost feel for smaller hands.

items.name: Sweeper — spiked index (variant of Grip 1)
items.grip: The inside-horseshoe sweeper with the index finger spiked into the ball so the middle finger pulls the seam unopposed.
items.movement: Slurve-adjacent — trades some HB for depth versus a pure flat sweeper.
items.when: The pronator's way into a sweeper: for a pitcher who can't get through the corner at release, spiking makes the side and top spin easier to produce.
items.watch: Expect some slurve drift — you're buying depth at the cost of pure sweep.

items.name: Sweeper — spiked index (variant of Grip 2)
items.grip: The outside-horseshoe sweeper with the index spiked — same spike logic as the inside-horseshoe variant, just the other seam contact.
items.movement: Same as the spiked inside-horseshoe: some HB given back for added depth.
items.when: For a pronator who prefers the outside-horseshoe hold and still needs the spike to reach the shape without getting around the ball.
items.watch: Same slurve drift caveat — it's a deeper, less purely lateral sweeper.

items.name: Sweeper — spiked index (variant of Grip 3)
items.grip: The split two-seam Whirlybird hold with the index spiked, combining the hands-off seam effect with spike leverage.
items.movement: The most seam-dependent of the spiked group, with a wide IVB range — the spike steers the axis while the split seams do the sweeping.
items.when: For a pronator who wants the grip-does-the-work Whirlybird but still can't get to the corner at release.
items.watch: Most seam-sensitive of the set — small orientation errors turn it into a random breaking ball instead of a sweeper.

items.name: Garrett Crochet — cranked sweeper (LHP)
items.grip: Two-seam orientation with the fingers set toward the horseshoe and the ball cranked outward in the hand, so the fingers are already on the side of the ball before release. Thumb under.
items.movement: Pre-setting the ball on the side of the hand orients the seams for SSW sweep without having to get around it at release — big glove-side break with fastball intent kept intact.
items.when: For a hard thrower who wants large sweep but doesn't want to sacrifice the heater delivery to get around the ball.
items.watch: Carries the usual sweeper platoon caveat, and a cranked hold can go inconsistent on cold days.

items.name: Emerson Hancock — spiked sweeper
items.grip: A standard sweeper seam orientation thrown with the index spiked — nail dug into the ball rather than laid flat — used here specifically to add downward bite, not for the usual spin-efficiency reason.
items.movement: The harder and lower of his two slider looks, sitting alongside a firmer straight slider. The spike buys the downward movement a flat, horizontal sweeper otherwise lacks.
items.when: For a lowered-slot pitcher whose sweeper runs too flat and needs the spike to add depth and turn it into a real weapon.
items.watch: Long adaptation — expect it to feel bad for weeks before it settles, and trading sweep for depth cuts the platoon edge against same-handed hitters.

items.name: Nick Sandlin — inverted-horseshoe loose sweeper
items.grip: Ball turned so the horseshoe is upside down, open end facing down, middle finger set on the seam on the right side of that shape. The hold is deliberately light — looser than most.
items.movement: Not documented, but the inverted horseshoe plus a loose hold lets him shape the pitch with wrist and hand orientation at release rather than with grip pressure, paired with a low, funky slot.
items.when: For a feel pitcher with a funky low slot who shapes the ball actively with the hand rather than letting a fixed grip set it.
items.watch: A loose grip plus active hand manipulation is a command risk and hard to repeat — this is a feel pitch, not a grip-does-the-work one.

groups.title: Gyro slider
groups.lede: Bullet-spin sliders and hard gyros. Horseshoe and spike sets that kill sweep and play tight off the fastball.

items.name: SL6 — Horseshoe Standard
items.grip: Fingers ride most of the horseshoe, no spike. A clean gyro hold that starts with minimal index pressure and throws like the fastball.
items.movement: 4-8 off the fastball as bullet spin. The same seam gives SSW help and turns into a sweeper if the release gets more around the ball.
items.when: A solid default gyro for pronators — no supination required to throw it, and it holds velo.
items.watch: Which shape you actually get leans heavily on the release, so log the measured result rather than trusting the grip name.

items.name: SL5 — Horseshoe Spike
items.grip: Fingers on the horseshoe with the index spiked. Start from minimal index pressure and add spike to bring in depth.
items.movement: 5-8 off the fastball in the gyro window; more spike buys more depth. Target is roughly under 5 inches of IVB and 0 to -5 HB for a RHP.
items.when: The pronator's recipe for a hard breaking ball without supinating — bullet spin with a touch of tilt from the spike.
items.watch: It won't produce big sweep, and that's the intent — reach elsewhere if you want glove-side HB.

items.name: SL4 — Standard Spike
items.grip: SL3 placement with the index fingertip dug into the leather. The middle finger stays on the seam and does the work while the spiked index gets out of the way.
items.movement: 6-9 off the fastball, tighter and deeper than SL3. Removing index interference shifts the spin direction down for more depth and a tighter gyro.
items.when: For a pitcher who wants the middle finger to own the spin and produce depth off a slider base.
items.watch: Spike depth depends on hand size, and heavy spike carries blister risk.

items.name: Edwin Díaz — hard gyro
items.grip: A standard gyro hold squeezed tight and thrown like a fastball — no manipulation at release.
items.movement: Around 89 with roughly 4 inches of IVB and -2 HB. A true bullet that plays on velo and shape separation, not on big break.
items.when: For a power arm who wants a hard, tight breaking ball he can throw with fastball intent and zero shaping.
items.watch: It needs elite velo to play — the same 4/-2 shape at 82 is a cement mixer.

items.name: Adrián Morejón — fingers in the middle of the ball
items.grip: Index and middle placed in the bare middle of the ball, no seam to hook or pull. With no seam to grab, there's nothing to manipulate.
items.movement: Bullet spin that lives on velo — removing the seam removed the urge to manipulate and added about a tick, up toward 88.
items.when: For a pitcher whose gyro suffers because he keeps trying to shape it — take the seam away and just throw it harder.
items.watch: Less seam means less SSW help, so the pitch depends on velo to play.

groups.title: Death ball / vertical slider
groups.lede: Vertical sliders / death balls — heavy downer shapes from gyro-leaning grips and low finger pressure.

items.name: Trevor Megill — death ball (small index spike)
items.grip: Start from a standard curve set and lift the index off the leather onto a shallow spike, middle finger on the seam, thumb underneath. The spike takes the index out of the steering business so the middle finger owns the axis.
items.movement: Near-zero HB with real drop — a gyro-dominant look that reads as pure depth, no sweep to tip it. Sits only a few ticks under the heater.
items.when: For a supinator who already gets on the outside of the ball and wants a hard, sweep-free put-away that stays inside the death-ball velo window.
items.watch: It only works at plus velocity; give back the extra mph and the same grip decays into a soft, hangable curve.

items.name: Death ball — variation 1
items.grip: Fingers tight together riding the seams up by the horseshoe, thumb tucked underneath, ball carried out toward the fingertips. The seam orientation is doing the shaping work, not the wrist.
items.movement: Cue-ball gyro spin that strips the HB and lets the pitch fall late — expect roughly a half-foot to three-quarters of drop with almost nothing sideways.
items.when: When you want a breaking ball that can only go down and you can drive gyro spin hard, inside about 10 mph of the fastball.
items.watch: Lose the velo and the gyro flattens into a straight, slow slider with no bite.

items.name: Death ball — top of the horseshoe
items.grip: Set the fingers on top of the horseshoe, middle finger on the seam with the index parked alongside it, thumb under. Same seam family as the pronator gyro slider, just finished with a touch more tilt to trade flat spin for drop.
items.movement: Reads as a gyro — any drift toward positive IVB confirms it — but the added tilt converts spin into a few extra inches of depth. Runs mid-single-digits off the fastball.
items.when: For the supinator who has the flat gyro and wants a slightly steeper, more vertical version off the same seam.
items.watch: Thin margin: too little tilt and it comes out as a slutter instead of a death ball.

items.name: Death ball — spiked variant
items.grip: Two-seam-side set with the index nail spiked into the leather, middle finger on the seam, thumb under. Spiking clears the index the way the Megill grip does and nudges the spin axis downward for depth.
items.movement: Cleaner downward tilt from the removed index interference, sitting six to ten off the fastball. Add spike pressure to add drop.
items.when: A supinator's grip: the spike shapes the axis, but the qualifying velo still has to come from getting outside the ball, which is why it stays a supinator pitch.
items.watch: Spike pressure is blister-prone and the whole grip is hand-size dependent.

groups.title: Curveball
groups.lede: Topspin shapes for depth. Standard, spiked, and horseshoe sets across the pronation-supination range.

items.name: CB1 — Standard curveball
items.grip: Middle and index side by side, middle finger on a seam and index on the leather next to it, thumb on the opposite seam. Bury the ball into the palm with little or no gap so you can load pressure, ring knuckle on the side and pinky off.
items.movement: High-efficiency topspin at roughly 1:00–2:00 tilt, dropping 12–18 off the fastball. The hand getting to the side lets the fingers pull down in front for clean vertical action.
items.when: The default curve for a supinator who can genuinely get on top and yank it down.
items.watch: It demands real supination; a pronator forcing this grip tends to leak into a loopy, slurvy shape.

items.name: CB2 — Horseshoe curveball
items.grip: Same finger placement as CB1 but worked onto the horseshoe so the seam sits under more of the finger. The extra seam contact gives some arms better feel and a firmer pull point.
items.movement: Same depth family as CB1, often a few hundred rpm more from the added grip on the seam.
items.when: For a pitcher who has the standard curve but wants more feel off the seam — worth a side-by-side against CB1.
items.watch: Moving onto the horseshoe can nudge the axis, so confirm your tilt hasn't drifted.

items.name: CB3 — Standard Spike (knuckle curve)
items.grip: CB1 placement with the index fingertip dug into the leather, or the knuckle set on the ball. Taking the index out of the equation lets the middle finger put maximum force into the spin.
items.movement: Sharper topspin and more depth than CB1, 10–16 off the fastball, with less HB because the index is no longer steering.
items.when: Often the way a pronator or smaller-handed arm finally finds a real, tight curve.
items.watch: Spike pressure is comfort- and blister-dependent — dial it in gradually.

items.name: CB4 — Horseshoe Spike
items.grip: Horseshoe orientation with the index spiked — the horseshoe feel of CB2 stacked with the spike leverage of CB3.
items.movement: CB3's tight downward shape with a touch more spin off the horseshoe.
items.when: For the arm that likes both the horseshoe seam and the index-off spike and wants them together.
items.watch: Same blister caveat as any spiked grip.

items.name: CB5 — Standard with index off
items.grip: CB1 set with the index lifted completely off the ball — a pure middle-finger curve with nothing beside it to interfere.
items.movement: The most vertical of the standard six, closest to true 12-6.
items.when: For a pitcher who gets more feel and consistency once the index is fully out of the way.
items.watch: The feel is unusual and command can wander until the grip is repped in.

items.name: CB6 — Horseshoe with index off
items.grip: Horseshoe orientation with the index off — the index-off idea of CB5 applied to the horseshoe seam.
items.movement: Same steep, near-12-6 shape as CB5.
items.when: For the index-off pitcher who prefers the feel of the horseshoe seam.

items.name: Paul Skenes — curveball
items.grip: Traditional set: middle finger along the seam on top of the ball, index alongside, thumb underneath, ball held out toward the fingertips.
items.movement: A pure depth look — the vertical breaking shape his sweeper and slider don't offer.
items.when: A useful case study in how a pronation-leaning arm still gets to a curve for an occasional different-shape offering.
items.watch: The least-used pitch in his mix, thrown rarely as a change of look rather than a workhorse.

items.name: Aaron Nola — spiked knuckle curve
items.grip: Index nail driven straight into the leather so the knuckle rides above the ball and the index adds no force, thumb on the middle of the seam right at the top edge, almost sitting on the middle finger. All the pressure lives at two points: the middle fingertip and the thumb tip. Because the spike lands on leather rather than a seam, it sits closer to a spiked slider than a classic spiked curve.
items.movement: Heavy topspin off a clean middle finger, giving late, tight downward bite rather than sweep — roughly 79–81 against a low-90s fastball.
items.when: A pronator's route to real depth, so it fits either bias; works as a primary put-away and a heavy-usage secondary.
items.watch: The two-point pressure is precise, so small thumb drift moves the shape a lot, and the spike is uncomfortable and blister-prone early. This is depth first, not a sweeping look.

items.name: Framber Valdez — angled-seam curveball (LHP)
items.grip: Thumb-dominant pressure with the ball set slightly angled against the seam rather than square on it, and the middle finger worked around to the front of the ball at release. That front-of-ball middle finger is what sets it apart from a two-fingers-on-top curve.
items.movement: Heavy 12-6 depth with no lift out of the hand, so it holds the fastball plane far longer than most curves before it dives.
items.when: When you want a curve you can land in the zone, off it, and to both halves rather than only as a chase pitch.
items.watch: Thumb-heavy pressure is a feel and blister risk, and the front-of-ball action needs you well out front — let the release drift back and it flattens.

items.name: Trent Thornton — hooked-finger two-seam curveball
items.grip: Ball set in a two-seam fastball orientation with the finger hooked onto the side of the seam instead of laid over the top — on the side, then hooked in even harder for a deep anchor. The thumb is the directional cue, thought of as coming over the center of the plate.
items.movement: The deep finger hook gives an extreme pull point, which is where the very high spin comes from.
items.when: For a supinator who can snap hard and wants a big-spin downer built off a fastball-look grip.
items.watch: Aggressive snapping plus the hooked finger taxes the elbow and the fingertip, and the hard-snap intent tends to cost command.

items.name: Justin Verlander — flipped-horseshoe curveball (ex-tucked knuckle curve)
items.grip: Index and middle together on smooth leather beside the horseshoe rather than riding it, thumb underneath. The original knuckle curve tucked the pointer flush against the ball; that version was dropped because a big-league ball blistered the tucked finger, and the grip was later flipped to the far side of the horseshoe. Only the hand placement changed — the release stayed the same.
items.movement: Re-orienting which seams the fingers cross re-shapes the pitch without asking the arm to do anything new.
items.when: A working example of changing shape by moving the hand on the ball while holding release constant — reach for the idea when a breaking ball goes sideways two in a row.
items.watch: The tucked version is a blister magnet with a real ball, and flipping horseshoes shifts both the curve and the slider, so the two have to be re-tuned together.

groups.title: Changeup
groups.lede: Cambios by mechanism — pronated turnover, seam-shifted wake, and kick/split variants for arms that will not turn it over.

items.name: Traditional changeup (two-seam, ring finger on seam)
items.grip: Two-seam orientation with the middle and ring fingers on the seams, index and pinky set off to the side and off the seams, thumb underneath. The ring finger is meant to carry the ball through release.
items.movement: Runs more than it drops, 8–12 off the fastball. Driving the ring finger through makes turning it over the natural finish.
items.when: The baseline pronator changeup — the standard starting point for an arm that turns the ball over easily.
items.watch: If you don't kill the backspin it floats, which is why supinators tend to stall out on this grip.

items.name: Circle changeup
items.grip: Index and thumb pinched into a circle on the side of the ball, the other three fingers resting on top. The circle pre-loads the pronated forearm angle so the middle finger can run through the side of the ball.
items.movement: Arm-side sidespin and tail, 8–12 off the fastball; extreme pronators can push HB past a foot and a half.
items.when: The pronator's changeup when you want heavy run and can genuinely turn it over.
items.watch: Tough on small hands and hard for a supinator to finish — the run just won't show up.

items.name: Paul Skenes — changeup (2025 grip)
items.grip: Fingers offset toward the side of the ball with less seam contact than his earlier college grip, held off the seams so the axis shifts.
items.movement: A hard, low-usage change that has missed a high rate of bats in limited looks.
items.when: An example of dialing a changeup by shifting the axis and backing off seam contact rather than changing the arm action.
items.watch: Still a show-me pitch behind the primary offspeed, so the sample is thin.

items.name: Logan Webb — seam-shifted split-change
items.grip: A split-change set: thumb, index and middle separated from the grouped ring and pinky, with the index and middle sitting far inside on the ball so the index catches more seam late in delivery. Screwball-adjacent finger position.
items.movement: Depth and arm-side run without pronating — roughly 9 inches of HB and a few inches of negative IVB — because the shape comes from finger position and seam-shifted wake, not turning it over.
items.when: For a supinator who won't pronate a changeup but wants one usable to both sides of the plate.
items.watch: Feel-dependent, and a lower arm slot helps the seam orientation do its job.

items.name: Tarik Skubal — seam-shifted changeup
items.grip: A two-seam changeup grip offset so one specific seam stays on top all the way through release. A common teaching aid is a paint dot inside the horseshoe — keep the dot on top.
items.movement: Big depth and fade generated by seam-shifted wake instead of wrist pronation; on a good one it tumbles down and away hard from a hitter-side start.
items.when: For an arm that admits it doesn't pronate well and needs depth from seam effect rather than turnover.
items.watch: The seam orientation has to be exact — roll the dot off top and it's a flat, straight fastball speed.

items.name: Clay Holmes — kick change
items.grip: A circle/two-seam base with the middle finger spiked — fingertip on the seam, knuckle raised — and the ring finger taking more of the ball. A big-handed, big-sweep supinator will spike shallower than a smaller-handed arm.
items.movement: Spiking makes the middle finger the last one off, kicking the axis toward a roughly 3:00 saucer spin so you get pronator-style depth without pronating.
items.when: The supinator's changeup — reach for it when you want turnover depth but can't turn the wrist over.
items.watch: Inconsistent until the feel is there: some days it comes out splitter-flat, some days like a lefty curve.

items.name: Baby kick change
items.grip: A two-seam grip slid back on the seams with the middle finger spiked down to about ring-finger length so middle and ring share the release, thumb under.
items.movement: Flat-to-negative IVB without pronating, 7–11 off the fastball. Bringing the ring finger in cuts spin efficiency while the raised middle finger kicks the axis over for arm-side depth.
items.when: A clean teaching version of the kick change for arms that can't pronate a circle change.
items.watch: Hand-size dependent — bigger hands spike more, smaller hands less.

items.name: Devin Williams — Airbender (Fosh circle change)
items.grip: A Fosh-circle set: middle and ring across the seams, index and thumb forming the circle, pinky tucked out of the release. Thrown off the middle and ring, off the seams.
items.movement: Extreme spin and better than a foot and a half of HB on nearly every one — it reads like a lefty sweeper out of a right hand.
items.when: The extreme pronator's changeup, natural for a low three-quarter slot that pronates hard.
items.watch: Harder to master than a straight change, since being off the seams removes the easy conduit for pronation.

items.name: Hunter Brown — split-change
items.grip: Index and middle split just outside a two-seam grip, ball set back in the hand, thumb tucked under, ring and pinky off to the side. The split kills spin so you don't have to turn it over.
items.movement: Fastball feel out of the hand with hard, tumbling depth as the split strips backspin.
items.when: For a power arm that wants a hard offspeed with fastball look and none of a true splitter's finger stress — the split does the work, so it fits either bias.
items.watch: A feel pitch: split width and how deep it sits decide whether it reads splitter or changeup.

items.name: Vulcan changeup
items.grip: Ball wedged deep into the V between the middle and ring fingers, index and middle on one side and ring and pinky on the other, thumb underneath. Held back like a split.
items.movement: Changeup fade with split-style depth, 8–12 off the fastball, because the finger split kills spin without any pronation.
items.when: For a pitcher who can't turn over a circle change but has the hand for a deep, wedged set.
items.watch: Awkward for small hands and rep-intensive to command; easy to slow down and dump velo if the hand decelerates with it.

items.name: Trevor Hoffman — palmball changeup
items.grip: Squeezed by the thumb and ring finger to force the ball back into the palm, index and middle resting on top without carrying it. The wrinkle: pinch the seam between thumb and index right at release.
items.movement: Big velocity separation created by hand pressure rather than spin, arriving soft with a late, gentle sink.
items.when: The classic case for killing velo through the palm rather than spin manipulation — a fastball-decline salvage pitch that lived on arm-speed disguise.
items.watch: Deep-in-the-palm grips cost command, and with almost no deceptive movement it lives or dies on velo separation off a fastball that sells it.

items.name: Cole Sulser — split-change (light side thumb)
items.grip: Held along the two seams, nearly a circle grip, but with a real split gap between index and middle, and the thumb kept light on the side of the ball instead of tucked all the way under.
items.movement: The two-seam split plus the light thumb drops spin sharply — several hundred rpm off a previous changeup grip — for more drag and more depth.
items.when: A circle-change-to-splitter hybrid for an arm chasing a big spin drop from a small grip change.
items.watch: Losing that much spin costs the tight fastball-mirroring look, and the light thumb costs command until it's repped.

items.name: Trevor Richards — four-seam ring-finger changeup
items.grip: A circle-change hand rotated to a four-seam orientation to get more depth across the seams, with no visible circle showing. The ring finger is the engine, kept on the ball as long as possible.
items.movement: High-spin, not low — near the top of the league for changeup spin — proving a changeup can miss bats without killing spin. The across-the-seams orientation makes the depth; the late ring finger sets the axis.
items.when: For a hard pronator who can't kill spin and would rather generate depth by staying on it and finishing out front.
items.watch: Pronation is the whole pitch, so turning it over early buries it — command-fragile, and not a fit for anyone chasing seam-shifted depth.

items.name: One-seam changeup
items.grip: Set so a single seam is the active contact point rather than riding both seams or sitting across the horseshoe. Tinker with pinky position and keep the overall hold on the loose side.
items.movement: Moves via seam effect at near-maximum spin efficiency rather than by killing spin — the opposite of the usual low-efficiency changeup design.
items.when: A good option for an arm that can't kill spin, or whose changeup keeps coming out as a firm, flat two-seam.
items.watch: Seam-effect pitches are orientation-sensitive, so any release inconsistency moves the seam and the movement wanders; velo separation has to come from the hand.

items.name: Claw changeup
items.grip: Thumb touches the pinky, which forces the index, middle and ring into a claw over the top of the ball. The ball sits back against the claw rather than on fingertip pressure — three fingers on top, thumb-pinky ring underneath for support.
items.movement: A third route to killing velo alongside the palmball and vulcan: taking the thumb off the bottom removes the main velocity-producing pressure point while three fingers on top add drag.
items.when: For an arm that wants velo reduction without burying the ball in the palm or splitting the fingers.
items.watch: Hand-size dependent, and pulling the thumb off the bottom costs stability and command — mostly a training-facility grip outside a few big-league examples.

groups.title: Splitter
groups.lede: Splits and splinkers. Spin-killed depth, from soft chase splitters to sinker-velocity power splinkers.

items.name: Splitter 1 — Standard
items.grip: Index and middle spread wide to the edges of a two-seam set, ball riding on the inside of the split rather than out on the fingertips. Thumb underneath for a stable shelf; ring and pinky ride off the side.
items.movement: Heavy tumble, 6-10 off the fastball and often under 1200 rpm. The wide split strips backspin, so spin efficiency drops and the ball dies vertically more than it fades — no Magnus lift to hold it up.
items.when: The default spin-kill offspeed for either bias, since the depth is friction and gravity, not forearm action. Reach for it when you want a true dead-drop under the zone.
items.watch: The wide split gates on hand size and finger flexibility, and it carries the family's finger and elbow load.

items.name: Splitter 2 — Standard with hiked thumb
items.grip: Same wide two-seam split, but the thumb climbs the side of the ball instead of shelving underneath.
items.movement: The same tumbling depth with a touch more arm-side fade than the flat-thumb version.
items.when: A feel adjustment for pitchers who command the pitch better with the thumb on the side; try it when the standard hold floats on you.
items.watch: Losing the thumb shelf costs support under the ball, so shape can wander inconsistent.

items.name: Splitter 3 — The Off-Set
items.grip: Standard split slid off-center toward the arm side (right for a RHP) so the fingers sit off the midline of the ball, freeing one finger to load more pressure.
items.movement: Splitter depth with added arm-side run — starts to take on the look of a split-change.
items.when: When you want some horizontal on the drop, or need the lopsided finger pressure for feel.
items.watch: Easy to slide all the way into a split-change and lose the true splitter tumble.

items.name: Splitter 4 — “The Gausman”
items.grip: More hand on top of the ball: ring and pinky come up alongside the split instead of parking off to the side, closer to a split-change hold. Let it leave off the inside of the fingers, not the tips.
items.movement: 7-10 off the fastball with hybrid shape — splitter depth stacked on changeup-style arm-side fade.
items.when: A more controlled, repeatable feel than the traditional split; fits an arm that wants both planes off the heater.
items.watch: Unorthodox hold — most splitters aren't carried this deep-handed, so it takes buy-in to trust.

items.name: Paul Skenes — splinker
items.grip: Index and middle split lightly on a two-seam set, sitting on the ball rather than wedged deep like a true split. Extra index pressure to drive the tail; thumb under.
items.movement: Splitter-grade depth at sinker velocity with arm-side run — the index pressure turns spin-kill drop into a heavy tailing sinker shape.
items.when: A pronation-leaning power arm that wants ground balls and whiffs off the fastball, thrown with sinker intent.
items.watch: Velo is the entry fee — down in the mid-80s it's just a firm splitter — and it carries splitter-family finger stress.

items.name: Jhoan Duran — splinker
items.grip: Fingers spread on the seams in a two-seam orientation, ball set fairly deep, thumb tucked to the side.
items.movement: Spin kill from the split, tail from the seams, all at near-fastball velo — depth and arm-side run with no speed given up.
items.when: Only makes sense for a true power arm; the whole pitch is built on throwing offspeed shape at the top of the velo band.
items.watch: Without elite velo the same shape is just a hittable sinker.

items.name: Ryan O'Rourke — splitter (index on seam)
items.grip: Wide split with the index finger set on a seam and the middle out on the leather, ball deep in the hand, thumb under. Pull through with the index.
items.movement: Consistent tumble — the seam under the index gives one finger a defined pull point, so the pitch bites instead of floating.
items.when: A teaching version for pitchers who lose feel with both fingers on smooth leather; the seam anchors the release.
items.watch: Still a wide split, so hand size and finger flexibility gate it.

items.name: Bryce Miller — splitter (middle finger on seam)
items.grip: Split with the middle finger on a seam and the index on the leather — the mirror of the index-on-seam hold. Thumb under; let the middle finger come off the seam last.
items.movement: Hard, tumbling depth that holds velo — the middle finger, usually the last one off the ball, gets a defined seam edge at release.
items.when: Fits a four-seam-heavy power arm that wants a firm offspeed thrown on fastball intent.
items.watch: Same hand-size caveat as any true split.

items.name: Fosh splitter
items.grip: Split set deeper toward the palm: index and middle straddle the ball, ring and pinky wrap up the side, thumb under, ball choked back. A close cousin of the deep-handed Gausman hold.
items.movement: 6-9 off the fastball — splitter depth with a hint of changeup fade, living between a change and a true split in both movement and look.
items.when: A landing spot when a true splitter is too inconsistent or a changeup won't get depth; the deep set kills spin but keeps feel for command.
items.watch: Deeper in the palm trades away the sharp late tumble, and it wants a big hand.

items.name: Kirby Yates — splitter (thumb pressure)
items.grip: A thumb-pressure split: the thumb, underneath or on the side, is an active pressure point rather than a passive shelf. The index/middle spread is individual — the feel lives in the thumb.
items.movement: Firm, around 87 with a few inches of arm-side movement — a tight, heavy-sinking offspeed that lives on ground balls and chase.
items.when: For a pitcher willing to tinker: lead with thumb pressure over finger spread and throw it with fastball arm speed.
items.watch: Highly individual — this one has to be found in the pen, not copied off a photo.

items.name: Roki Sasaki — splitter (2026 grip)
items.grip: Narrower spread than his forkball, ball moved out onto the fingertips instead of the crotch of the fingers, and rotated from four-seam to a two-seam orientation.
items.movement: About 5 harder than the fork version with less total break but a sharper, later, more repeatable bite and more arm-side run.
items.when: When you need velo and consistency over raw break — fingertips plus a two-seam set is the trade toward a firmer, commandable splitter.
items.watch: Buys control by giving up total break; it's effectively the tighter twin of his forkball.

groups.title: Forkball
groups.lede: Deep-wedge forks. Maximum spin kill and tumble for arms with the finger spread to hold them.

items.name: Forkball — classic deep wedge
items.grip: Index and middle spread as wide as the hand allows with the ball jammed deep between them, further back than a splitter, thumb square underneath. Thrown fastball-hard with a downward wrist snap right at release.
items.movement: Very low spin — the deep wedge blocks the fingers from putting backspin on the ball, so it tumbles closer to 12-6 than a fastball and gravity wins early. A touch slower than a same-arm splitter.
items.when: When you want maximum spin-kill depth and have the finger length to wedge it; the drop is friction, not forearm, so it fits either bias.
items.watch: The forced wide split loads the elbow and the snap loads wrist and forearm; command trails a splitter, and it needs long fingers.

items.name: Kodai Senga — ghost fork
items.grip: Hand spread wide, index on the outside edge of a seam, thumb on a different seam, middle laid across the heart of the horseshoe. Set deep enough to kill spin but deliberately short of a true forkball's jam to the base of the fingers.
items.movement: Low spin near 1,160 rpm off a fastball that touches the upper 90s — over three feet of drop with real arm-side break. Tunnels off the heater, then dies.
items.when: A fastball-tunnel chase pitch for a power arm; the deep-but-not-jammed set keeps the movement without the full load of a true deep wedge.
items.watch: Stopping short of the wedge is a deliberate durability choice, and as a chase pitch it bleeds walks when hitters lay off.

items.name: Roki Sasaki — forkball
items.grip: Extra-wide split with the ball lodged firmly down between the fingers in a four-seam orientation — the near-zero-spin version.
items.movement: Slow with more total break, and the movement turns chaotic — nearly knuckleball, breaking any direction — because four-seam plus a deep lodge maximizes spin kill.
items.when: When you want maximum spin kill and unpredictable movement and can live without any command.
items.watch: Can't be commanded, and it's the higher-stress grip — the reason he moved toward the tighter splitter.

groups.title: Cutter
groups.lede: Small, late glove-side shapes that keep four-seam-family spin — riders through two-seam depth variants.

items.name: CT1 — Standard cutter (four-seam offset)
items.grip: Four-seam grip with the fingers tight together, pads on the seams, shifted toward the pinky side of the ball. Thumb under or just off-center, ring on the side, pinky off.
items.movement: 2-5 off the fastball, keeping most of the ride. The pinky-side offset lays a dose of sidespin over the backspin, so it cuts glove-side late at 95-98% of fastball velo.
items.when: The easiest cutter to add for a supinator and a common quick fix for a pronator who wants something glove-side; throw it on fastball intent.
items.watch: Manipulate it and you bleed velo without buying break — keep the fastball intent.

items.name: CT2 — Standard Between (two-seam)
items.grip: Two-seam orientation, index and middle riding between the seams, offset slightly off-center.
items.movement: 3-5 off the fastball — a little less ride and a touch more cut than the four-seam offset.
items.when: When a pitcher gets better feel for cut from between the seams; the same off-center principle on a two-seam set.
items.watch: A two-seam set can pick up seam-shifted wake and drift toward slutter shape.

items.name: CT3 — Standard Around (two-seam, up the ball)
items.grip: Two-seam orientation with the fingers up the ball toward the horseshoe and off the midline, giving more seam to get around.
items.movement: 4-7 off the fastball, into slutter territory — bigger glove-side break than the tighter cutters.
items.when: The supinator's cutter that leans toward a slutter when you want more sweep than a true cut.
items.watch: Easy to overcook into a slow slider; dropping the thumb more under the ball pulls it back toward cutter shape, and watch the velo.

items.name: Kenley Jansen — riding cutter
items.grip: Closer to a slider hold: index and middle pressed together, middle finger riding the long seam, index alongside, thumb rotated further around the ball than a four-seam. Grip it like a slider, throw it like a fastball.
items.movement: The rare cutter that rides as much as it cuts — unusual carry with a late glove-side bite at fastball velo.
items.when: When you want a cutter that holds the fastball's ride; finish through it and get around the side just slightly.
items.watch: Demands the most pronation discipline of the cutter grips or it tips into true slider territory.

items.name: Mariano Rivera — four-seam cutter
items.grip: Four-seam fastball grip tilted slightly outward so the fingers get onto the side of the ball while it still feels like a heater, with extra middle-finger pressure.
items.movement: Late glove-side cut carrying true four-seam rotation, held at 95-98% of fastball velo — a small, sharp break, not a sweep.
items.when: The template for the standard cutter: lead with middle-finger pressure and a strong finish, keeping four-seam spin rather than breaking-ball spin.
items.watch: The break is small by design — it misses barrels, not bats.

items.name: Corbin Burnes — four-seam cutter
items.grip: Fingers on the four-seam horseshoe, offset to the pinky side, thumb underneath, with pronounced middle-finger pressure — the same family as the standard cutter.
items.movement: Around 95 with a few inches of glove-side break — fastball intent with a late cut, thrown hard enough to bore in on lefties and hold velo.
items.when: A supinator's primary fastball, but this standard-cutter family isn't supinator-only; throw it like the heater.
items.watch: Wants long fingers and a big hand, and overdoing the offset drifts it toward a slutter.

items.name: Drew Rasmussen — cutter (high thumb)
items.grip: Fingers together on top of the ball, offset to the pinky side, ball choked fairly deep. The signature is a thumb riding high on the side of the ball instead of tucked under. Standard four-seam-offset family.
items.movement: Late glove-side cut at fastball velo — the high thumb shifts the axis the ball leaves on and keeps a supinator on the outside of the ball without any wrist manipulation.
items.when: A cutter-first look for a supinator whose whole arsenal lives on that side of the ball; think fastball and let the offset do the cutting.
items.watch: Read off an in-game frame, so the finger detail is approximate.

items.name: Cutter from a standard breaking-ball grip
items.grip: A breaking-ball grip (fingers together on the seam toward the horseshoe) backed off toward the fastball — held shallower and more on top of the ball than a slider, thumb under.
items.movement: 3-5 off the fastball, still inside the heater's window: the seam supplies the cut, so the ball comes out with fastball spin plus a small glove-side break.
items.when: Likely the best cutter route for a pronator — the seam does the cutting, so you never have to get around the ball.
items.watch: Still fighting the natural bias; expect less velo than a gyro-based option.

items.name: Cam Schlittler — 2025 cutter (slower, more depth)
items.grip: A breaking-ball grip devolved into a cutter, held deep: fingers together along the seam toward the horseshoe, offset, with more finger on the side of the ball. In-game frame.
items.movement: More depth but less velo, closer to a slutter than a fastball variant — the deep set trades ride for drop.
items.when: The before picture of a grip-depth experiment; useful for seeing what holding the breaking-ball grip deep gives you.
items.watch: Loses the fastball window — the extra depth costs velo and ride.

items.name: Cam Schlittler — 2026 cutter (harder, more ride)
items.grip: Same offset breaking-ball-to-cutter hold with the fingers moved up toward the top of the ball and out toward the fingertips, offset staying on the pinky side. In-game frame.
items.movement: Keeps the four-seam ride and adds velo while the offset still supplies the cut — a shallower grip that plays harder with more carry than the deeper 2025 version.
items.when: The after picture of the same experiment: move the fingers up and out to trade depth back for velo and ride. Keep it in the fingertips, think fastball.
items.watch: Less depth than the deeper version by design.

groups.title: Sinker / two-seam
groups.lede: Two-seamers and one-seam sinkers. Symmetric run through seam-shifted, wake-driven dive.

items.name: FT1 — Standard two-seam / sinker
items.grip: Index and middle ride both narrow seams in a two-seam orientation; for the sinker version slide the index a touch inward toward the middle of the ball. Thumb underneath or a hair off-center, ring finger bracing the side, pinky clear.
items.movement: Sits within a mph of the four-seam, and release decides the shape: stay through it up top and it runs, get over the top down in the zone and it dives.
items.when: The default arm-side fastball for pronators, who roll over it naturally; a supinator can borrow the same grip and let seam orientation supply the run instead of the wrist.
items.watch: From a high slot it wants to cut instead of run, which is the cue to accept a gyro two-seam rather than force arm-side life.

items.name: FT2 — Close two-seam
items.grip: Same two-seam orientation with index and middle pressed together on the seams, consolidating everything into one pressure point for feel.
items.movement: Runs more than it sinks and holds velo the best of the family.
items.when: Reach for it when you want speed and a clean feel over depth; it still works for a supinator when the seam does the sinking rather than the hand.
items.watch: Fingers close together means less leverage, so expect less run than the spread grips give you.

items.name: FT3 — Wide two-seam
items.grip: Two-seam orientation with the index and middle spread wide across the seams.
items.movement: Gives up a mph or two and reads as more sink as it drifts toward split shape.
items.when: When you want extra depth and can trade a little velocity for it.
items.watch: The line between this and a split-change is thin; the drop comes from killing spin and speed.

items.name: Zach Britton — one-seam sinker (LHP)
items.grip: Index and middle tight together riding a single inside seam, thumb under, with the ball turned so the opposite seam sits out of the airflow.
items.movement: Dives and runs far past what the spin axis predicts; the asymmetric wake off the exposed seam does the work, not Magnus.
items.when: The reference one-seam sinker and a genuine route for supinators, since the seam handles the pronation the wrist otherwise would.
items.watch: Deeply feel-dependent, and it pairs the grip with a specific delivery; a small orientation miss collapses it back into an ordinary two-seamer.

items.name: Blake Treinen — one-seam sinker
items.grip: Fingers together with the pads on one seam near the top of the ball, thumb under, choked fairly deep.
items.movement: Arm-side dive that comes from seam orientation rather than a rolled-over wrist.
items.when: A standing example for a supinator with a big sweeper who wants a diving fastball without changing how he releases it.
items.watch: Carries the same orientation sensitivity as every one-seamer.

items.name: Joe Musgrove — one-seam sinker
items.grip: Index and middle straddle a single seam with the index set slightly ahead, thumb under on the lower seam.
items.movement: Picks up run and sink the spin doesn't explain because one seam trips the airflow on a single side of the ball in flight.
items.when: The clean template for the seam-driven sinker family; it suits either bias, supinators especially.
items.watch: Won't survive every arm slot, since high slots tend to cut the two-seam orientation instead.

items.name: Shuuto
items.grip: Held like a two-seamer, with the index set between the seams and the middle roughly halfway down the side. The shape comes from pressure, not geometry: drive heavy index-finger pressure through release to tilt the axis.
items.movement: Fastball-adjacent velocity with sharp, late arm-side and downward break that bores in on a same-handed hitter.
items.when: A contact pitch built to jam and break bats inside rather than miss them, and a right-handed staple in Japan.
items.watch: Pressure-driven, so it's erratic until the feel is grooved, and it invites the barrel; a miss over the middle gets hurt.

items.name: Tayler Saucedo — one-seam sinker from a low slot (LHP)
items.grip: A one-seam hold that splits the seams, the fingers sitting on a single seam rather than riding both tracks of a conventional two-seamer.
items.movement: Plays like a right-hander's slider thrown left-handed: heavy sweep with sink.
items.when: A low-slot, left-handed entry in the one-seam family; seam-driven, so it fits either bias.
items.watch: Slot-locked, since over the top the same grip dives uncontrollably and can't be commanded; it can take years to tame.

groups.title: Four-seam fastball
groups.lede: Four-seam grips and the finger/seam tweaks that move ride, cut, and run at the top of the zone.

items.name: FF1 — Standard four-seam
items.grip: Index and middle laid across the horseshoe with the pads on the seams, a finger's width apart. Thumb flat or tucked underneath, ring finger on the side or under depending on hand size, pinky off.
items.movement: The baseline: 90%-plus spin efficiency and clean ride, with less HB out of higher slots. Pronating earlier lifts efficiency further.
items.when: The recommended starting point for any backspin- or pronation-biased arm chasing IVB and carry.
items.watch: Little movement by design; it plays on velo, extension and ride.

items.name: FF2 — Close grip
items.grip: Index and middle side by side or pressed together on the center of the ball, concentrating pressure through the middle finger.
items.movement: A cut-ride shape as efficiency slips toward the 80-90% range.
items.when: A natural cut-ride fastball for supinators who can't push efficiency up.
items.watch: The wrong direction if you want pure ride; it trades efficiency for cut.

items.name: FF3 — Wide grip
items.grip: Index and middle spread wider across the top of the ball than FF1, still sitting on the seams.
items.movement: Close to FF1, though some lose about a mph and some gain command, with a slight lean toward cut.
items.when: A comfort and command option for bigger hands.
items.watch: Wider fingers can bleed a little velo, so keep an eye on the radar.

items.name: Tyler Glasnow — wide-finger cut-ride four-seam
items.grip: FF3 taken to its extreme: held wide with curved fingers wrapping the ball rather than sitting flat on top, so one finger rides off-center on the side and creates the cut.
items.movement: A tall, extension-heavy fastball that plays as cut-ride; the cut dials in and out by where the hand sits, not by the grip.
items.when: For a supinator whose hand wants to be on the side of it, letting the natural cut make a big fastball read as a shape hitters don't expect.
items.watch: Cut is the default rather than a switch; you give up true arm-side ride, and the straight version takes active hand repositioning.

items.name: Félix Bautista — two-seam-oriented four-seam
items.grip: Seams rotated so only two cross the front of the ball in flight, yet backspin stays near-perfect: keep the fingers behind the ball and roll it off the fingertips with no wrist snap in either direction.
items.movement: Extreme ride with minimal drop, among the flattest fastballs in the game despite the non-standard orientation.
items.when: For an arm that naturally sets off-axis and gets told it's gripping wrong; four-seam is a spin classification, not a grip requirement, so any arm that stays behind the ball can carry it.
items.watch: Only works on a genuinely clean release; any wrist snap on the rotated orientation turns ride into unintended seam-shifted movement.

groups.title: Modifiers — apply to any grip
groups.lede: Grip knobs — spike, thumb position, tilt, and depth — layered onto any base grip to shift its shape.

items.name: Spike — curl
items.grip: Curl the index under rather than digging it fully into the leather, which adds middle-finger pressure without the full fingertip spike.
items.movement: Nudges spin direction down a few degrees: roughly 1-3" more depth on a breaking ball with little change to HB.
items.when: A half-step toward a spike when you want a bit more depth but aren't ready to commit to the full dig.
items.watch: Less axis shift than a full spike.

items.name: Spike — full
items.grip: Index fingertip dug into the leather, taking the index off the ball's spin contribution.
items.movement: 3-6" more depth on a slider or curve, with HB typically dropping 1-3"; backing the spike off reverses it and pushes spin upward.
items.when: Add spike progressively to build depth, or take it off when a curve is drifting toward slider.
items.watch: Blisters, and how far you can spike depends on hand size.

items.name: Spike — index off
items.grip: Lift the index fully off the ball for a pure middle-finger pitch.
items.movement: Like a full spike or a bit more: 4-7" of added depth with tighter HB.
items.when: When you want the maximum removal of index influence.
items.watch: Command can suffer and the feel is unusual.

items.name: Spike — index stacked
items.grip: Stack the index on top of the middle finger, loading the middle while keeping the index in contact for feel.
items.movement: Modest: 1-3" tighter HB and a small depth gain, more a feel and command change than a shape change.
items.when: When you want to concentrate pressure on the middle finger but keep index feedback.
items.watch: Rare in games, so log the results before you commit to it.

items.name: Thumb — 0 (under)
items.grip: Set the thumb directly underneath the ball.
items.movement: Pulls a breaking ball toward cutter shape: +2 to +5" IVB, 2-5" less HB, and often a tick of velo.
items.when: When you want to stay through the ball at release and turn a slider toward a cutter.
items.watch: Fights the around-the-ball feel a sweeper needs.

items.name: Thumb — 25
items.grip: Thumb a quarter of the way toward the side of the ball.
items.movement: The neutral reference position, with minimal movement change.
items.when: The most common comfort spot and the baseline to measure other thumb positions against.

items.name: Thumb — 50 (side)
items.grip: Move the thumb onto the side of the ball.
items.movement: Pushes toward slider and sweeper shape: 2-5" more HB, 1-3" less IVB, often down a mph.
items.when: When you want it easier to get around the ball and drive a cutter into a slider.
items.watch: Less support under the ball, so velo can leak.

items.name: Thumb — flat vs tucked
items.grip: Tuck the thumb tight under the ball, or lay it flat so the ball sits deeper in the hand.
items.movement: Tuck adds +2 to +4" IVB and a tick of velo; flat gives a few inches more depth.
items.when: Tuck when you want ride and velo, flat when you want the ball to sit deep for depth.
items.watch: The tuck can pull the pitch toward cutter shape.

items.name: Tilt — outward
items.grip: Rotate the base grip outward, which changes seam orientation and how the fingers come off the ball.
items.movement: On two-seam orientations, 2-5" more arm-side or glove-side HB via seam-shifted wake; small change on four-seam grips.
items.when: Small outward tilts to add SSW sweep on a two-seam-oriented slider.
items.watch: Easy to overdo, so verify the shape on your tracking data.

items.name: Tilt — inward
items.grip: Rotate the base grip inward, the opposite adjustment.
items.movement: 2-5" less HB and a slightly tighter shape.
items.when: When you want to kill some horizontal and tighten the pitch.

items.name: Depth — shallow vs deep
items.grip: Shallow sets the ball out on the fingertips; deep chokes it back into the hand.
items.movement: Shallow adds 1-2 mph and a touch more ride; deep costs 1-2 mph but adds feel and more depth on offspeed.
items.when: Shallow for velo and ride, deep for feel and depth; a slider usually rides shallower than a curve.
items.watch: Hand size drives this more than intent.
